prompt: Who writes the source address in an IP packet?
hint: Does anything in IP check it?

choices.text: The first router, from the interface the packet arrived on
choices.why: Routers forward the field as they find it.

choices.text: The sender
choices.why: Right. And nothing in IP checks what it wrote.

choices.text: The firewall, once it has checked the routing table
choices.why: A firewall can check it, but it does not write it.

choices.text: The receiver's IP layer, from the Ethernet header
choices.why: The receiver reads what the sender put there.

prompt: remote sent a request to the shop from 192.168.20.99 and curl timed out, yet the SYN reached www. Why did it time out?
hint: Where did www send its answer?

choices.text: fw dropped the SYN at the edge
choices.why: The recording on www shows the SYN arrived.

choices.text: www answered 192.168.20.99, an address that is not on the internet
choices.why: Right. The answer went nowhere useful.

choices.text: www refuses connections from the servers range
choices.why: It answered; the answer just went elsewhere.

choices.text: The certificate did not name the forged address
choices.why: The handshake never got as far as TLS.

prompt: Match each use of a forged source address to why it works.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.left: getting past a rule that trusts an address
pairs.right: the rule believes the source field
the answers go to the forged address, the victim

pairs.left: hiding where a flood comes from
pairs.right: each packet claims a different, random source

right_distractors: the switch learns the wrong port for a MAC

prompt: After the anti-spoofing rules were loaded, how many packets of the forged request did the private-sources rule drop?
hint: The counter on the first rule.

prompt: What does the rule fib saddr . iif oif missing drop?
hint: It asks the routing table a question about the source.

choices.text: Packets whose source is in a private range
choices.why: That is the first rule, which needs a list.

choices.text: Packets whose destination has no route out of fw
choices.why: It looks at the source, not the destination.

choices.text: Packets whose source is not reachable back through the interface they came in on
choices.why: Right. That is reverse path filtering.

choices.text: Replies to connections fw has not seen
choices.why: That is connection tracking's job.

prompt: A firewall has two internet providers, and some traffic arrives through one and leaves through the other. Which rp_filter value fits it?
hint: Which mode drops real customers there?

choices.text: 1, strict, as a firewall like fw should use
choices.why: Strict drops traffic that returns by the other provider.

choices.text: 2, loose
choices.why: Right. Any route back will do.

choices.text: 0, with the fib rule doing the same check
choices.why: The fib rule is the strict check, with the same problem.

choices.text: 1, because it acts on packets from private ranges alone
choices.why: It applies to every source, private or not.

prompt: What does BCP 38 ask every network to do?
hint: Which direction?

choices.text: Drop incoming packets from private ranges
choices.why: That protects you from what arrives.

choices.text: Drop outgoing packets whose source is not one of its own
choices.why: Right. It protects everybody else.

choices.text: Refuse to resolve names for strangers
choices.why: That is not being an open resolver.

choices.text: Sign its DNS zone
choices.why: That is DNSSEC.

prompt: laptop tried to reach the internet from 198.51.100.7 and fw dropped 1 packet. Which rule caught it?
hint: Which rule's counter moved?

choices.text: The private-sources rule, since the address is not the LAN's
choices.why: That rule matches on eth0 and private ranges; 198.51.100.7 is neither.

choices.text: The fib rule, the same one that stopped the forged request
choices.why: Right. fw has no route to it through the LAN interface.

choices.text: A separate BCP 38 rule in forward
choices.why: No new rule was added.

choices.text: NAT, which rewrote it
choices.why: NAT would have sent it on, not dropped it.

prompt: Behind NAT, towards the internet there is one legitimate source: the firewall's public ___.
hint: The last paragraph of the section.

prompt: A LAN machine is taken over and told to join somebody's flood with forged sources. What does the egress filter give the company?
hint: Two things: one for the victim, one for the defenders.

choices.text: The malware is removed from the machine
choices.why: A filter on fw does nothing to the laptop's software.

choices.text: The machine's honest traffic is blocked as well, until it is cleaned
choices.why: Without the forged address laptop connected normally.

choices.text: Its forged packets stop at fw, and a counter shows the attempt
choices.why: Right. Useless for the flood, and visible.

choices.text: The victim is told which machine is attacking
choices.why: The dropped packets do not reach the victim.

prompt: Why is a false answer in a resolver's cache worth more to an attacker than one forged reply to one client?
hint: Who reads the cache?

choices.text: Everybody who asks there is sent it until the entry expires
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The cache keeps it after the TTL runs out
choices.why: It lasts as long as the TTL allows.

choices.text: A cached answer bypasses DNSSEC
choices.why: A validating resolver checks before caching.

choices.text: The resolver sends it to other resolvers
choices.why: It serves its own clients.

prompt: The resolver's source port is known and its transaction IDs are random. What chance does one forged answer have of carrying the right ID?
hint: The ID is 16 bits.

choices.text: 1 in 16
choices.why: 16 is the number of bits, not of values.
That would be a 32-bit ID.
Right. 2 to the 16th.
That is 8 bits.

prompt: Which defences make a forged DNS answer less likely to be accepted, without checking the answer itself? Choose all that apply.
hint: One entry in the table checks the answer itself.

choices.text: Random transaction IDs
choices.why: Right. The forger has to guess one in 65,536.

choices.text: Random source ports
choices.why: Right. They multiply the guessing.

choices.text: DNSSEC
choices.why: DNSSEC checks the answer itself, so a forgery is useless.

choices.text: Not being an open resolver
choices.why: Right. Strangers cannot choose when it asks.

prompt: One laptop resolves the shop to a strange address; its neighbours, using the same resolver, get the right one. Where would you look first?
hint: Who else would a poisoned resolver affect?

choices.text: The shared resolver's cache
choices.why: A poisoned cache would mislead the neighbours too.

choices.text: The zone's DNSSEC signatures, which have expired
choices.why: That gives SERVFAIL to everybody, not a strange address.

choices.text: Its own hosts file and DNS settings
choices.why: Right. One machine differing from its neighbours points to something local.

choices.text: The transaction IDs the resolver has been using lately
choices.why: A race won against the resolver would reach its other clients.

prompt: Match each part of DNSSEC in the lab to what it is.
hint: The first paragraphs of the section.

pairs.right: the signature over a set of records
the resolver's word that it checked the signature
the key Unbound trusts without asking anybody

prompt: The lab has no root zone. How does Unbound on laptop come to trust the company's zone?
hint: Look at the configuration grep.

choices.text: It fetches the root's key from the internet at start-up
choices.why: The lab has no root to chain from.

choices.text: It is given the zone's key as a trust anchor
choices.why: Right. The chain, cut short.

choices.text: It trusts whatever the stub address serves
choices.why: The stub says where to ask, not what to believe.

choices.text: It asks the parent zone for a fingerprint of the key
choices.why: That is the internet's way; the lab has no parent.

prompt: A laptop uses a validating resolver elsewhere on the network and reads the ad flag. What is still unprotected?
hint: Who checked the signature, and who is trusting their word?

choices.text: The signature, because ad hides the RRSIG
choices.why: The RRSIG is shown beside the answer.

choices.text: The zone's private key, which the resolver holds
choices.why: The resolver holds the public key; the owner keeps the private one.

choices.text: The path, because ad is signed by the zone
choices.why: ad is a flag the resolver sets, not a signature.

choices.text: The hop between the two, unless it uses DNS over TLS or HTTPS
choices.why: Right. A forged ad on that hop would be believed.

prompt: After the address was changed without re-signing, what did laptop's dig receive?
hint: Look at the status line.

choices.text: 203.0.113.66, without the ad flag
choices.why: The resolver handed over no address at all.

choices.text: 192.0.2.80, from the cache
choices.why: The cached answer had been flushed.

choices.text: SERVFAIL, and no address
choices.why: Right. Validation failed, so nothing was handed on.

choices.text: NXDOMAIN, as if the name did not exist
choices.why: The name exists; its signature failed.

prompt: Why did dig +cd print 203.0.113.66 when the plain query failed?
hint: cd stands for something.

choices.text: +cd asks the resolver to skip validation
choices.why: Right. Checking disabled.

choices.text: +cd asks the zone's server directly, past Unbound
choices.why: It still asked 127.0.0.1.

choices.text: +cd bypasses the cache, and the cache held the SERVFAIL
choices.why: The difference is the check, not the cache.

choices.text: The signature had been fixed in between
choices.why: Nobody re-signed the zone.

prompt: The lab's signatures are valid until 31 December 2026. If nobody re-signs the zone, what do validating clients get on 1 January 2027?
hint: What does a mistake look like?

choices.text: The answers as before, but without ad
choices.why: A failed check gives no answer, not an unmarked one.

choices.text: The last cached addresses, until somebody re-signs
choices.why: Cached entries expire with their TTL of 300 seconds.

choices.text: SERVFAIL for the zone's names
choices.why: Right. An expired signature fails like a forged one.

choices.text: The answers as before; the date is advisory
choices.why: The resolver checks the validity dates.

prompt: Order what happened when laptop asked for the tampered name, from first to last.
hint: The log line and the status line.
items: Unbound fetches the answer from dns on port 5300
it checks the RRSIG against the zone's key
the signature does not match the changed address
dig gets SERVFAIL and no address
trap: The client hears nothing until the check has been made.

prompt: Forged DNS answers arrive from the internet at fw's eth0, claiming to come from 192.168.20.53, the company's internal DNS server. Which rule in this lesson drops them first?
hint: Which rule comes first in prerouting, and what does it match?

choices.text: The fib rule, since the source lives behind another interface
choices.why: It would, but the rule above it matches first.

choices.text: The private-sources rule on eth0
choices.why: Right. 192.168.0.0/16 never arrives from the internet.

choices.text: DNSSEC validation on the resolver
choices.why: It would refuse them, but later, after fw has let them in.

choices.text: rp_filter on fw's eth0
choices.why: fw has rp_filter at 0.

prompt: The company signs its zone. A member of staff at a hotel uses the hotel's resolver, which does not validate. What does the signing do for them?
hint: Who checks a signature?

choices.text: The laptop refuses forged answers by itself
choices.why: Checking is the validating resolver's job.

choices.text: It hides the question from the hotel's network
choices.why: DNSSEC hides nothing.

choices.text: Nothing: their resolver does not check it
choices.why: Right. A signature nobody checks protects nobody.

choices.text: Forged answers reach them as SERVFAIL
choices.why: SERVFAIL for a bad signature comes from a validating resolver.
